classification.reason: The coach provides executable cues and video-check instructions, such as intuiting the swing as accelerating the hand all the way to contact rather than stopping far from the ball, and checking 60 fps / 120 fps video frame counts before contact.

problem.title_as_question: Why Should You Think of Starting Your Forehand Swing at Contact?
problem.definition: Players often stop accelerating their hand too early before contact, releasing the wrist's elastic spring prematurely, which leaks energy, diminishes power, and causes loss of directional control.

symptoms.description: Racket wrist spring releases too early, taking 6 frames or more at 60 fps (12+ frames at 120 fps) before contact.
Loss of shot control, spraying balls wide or long, and hitting with reduced pace.
Lack of effortless power crack sensation, feeling like slow-twitch muscles must manipulate the racket.

causes.statement: The player fails to accelerate the hand all the way toward the ball, causing the wrist spring to release prematurely ahead of contact.
When the wrist spring releases prematurely, the brain compensates with slow-twitch muscle flexing to manipulate string face angle.
Elastic energy loaded in the wrist leaks out linearly with every millisecond the release window is extended beyond the ideal 40ms.

angles.summary: The racket overtaking the hand occurs across roughly 40 milliseconds (3 frames at 60 fps or 5-6 frames at 120 fps) before contact.
Two audio pops spaced 0.04 seconds apart illustrate how imperceptibly close spring release is to contact.
Players intuitively imagine a wide delay between hand acceleration stopping and contact, whereas kinetically it is almost simultaneous.
Pros like Federer, Alcaraz, and Raducanu release the spring exactly 3 frames before contact at 60 fps, while mistiming on a running ball releases earlier.
Student Amelia improved her wrist release duration from 12 frames at 120 fps down to 5-6 frames, transforming her power and crispness.

solutions.summary: Inspect 60 fps video at contact and press the backward key three times to verify whether wrist spring begins releasing within a 3-frame window.
solutions.external_goal: Step back three frames from contact in 60 fps video stats to see if the spring is just releasing.

solutions.summary: Think of the swing as starting at contact so that hand acceleration does not halt early.
Intuit the swing as accelerating all the way to contact rather than trying to micromanage a 40ms timing gap.
Drive through the kinetic chain using chest press, hip rotation, and a solid base to keep accelerating the hand deep into contact before letting the racket snap.
solutions.external_goal: Keep hand accelerating until right next to the ball before snapping.
